culture:Girona Cathedral.name: Girona Cathedral (Santa Maria)
culture:Girona Cathedral.teaser: Almost 23 metres of vault with no pillar to hold it: the widest Gothic nave anywhere
culture:Girona Cathedral.story: For about half a century the chapter argued over how to roof the church: three aisles, as everyone built, or one daring span. In 1417 the architect Guillem Bofill won, and the single vault went up 22.98 metres wide and 35 high, a width among church naves beaten only by St Peter's in Rome. Six hundred years later it has not moved. Outside, 90 Baroque steps laid in 1607 climb from the square; in September 2015 a Game of Thrones crew filmed Jaime Lannister riding his horse up them to the Great Sept of Baelor.
culture:Girona Cathedral.why: Walk to the middle of the nave and look up: the absence of columns is the whole point.
facts: Plaça de la Catedral, at the top of the Barri Vell

culture:Basílica de Sant Feliu.name: Basílica de Sant Feliu
culture:Basílica de Sant Feliu.teaser: Eight carved Roman and early-Christian tombs built into one presbytery wall, and usually nobody looking
culture:Basílica de Sant Feliu.story: Before the cathedral took the title, this was Girona's great church, raised over the grave of the martyr Felix, killed in 304. You can read its age in layers: a Romanesque core, a Gothic nave, a Baroque front, and in 2011 Benedict XVI made it a minor basilica. The reason to step in is in the presbytery. Eight sarcophagi of the 3rd and 4th centuries, Roman and early Christian, are set into the walls; no other church in Iberia shows a run like it. The saint linked to the flies legend lies here too; that story has its own card.
culture:Basílica de Sant Feliu.why: Stand close to the presbytery wall: the tombs are within arm's reach, carved some seventeen centuries ago.
facts: Plaça de Sant Feliu, at the foot of the Pujada de Sant Domènec, below the cathedral

culture:Sant Pere de Galligants.name: Sant Pere de Galligants
culture:Sant Pere de Galligants.teaser: A Benedictine church of the 1100s, now the Girona home of Catalonia's archaeology museum
culture:Sant Pere de Galligants.story: The monastery is first named in 988, but the church you enter dates from the first half of the 12th century, crowned by an octagonal bell tower ringed with Lombard bands. It has been a museum since 1857 and is now the Girona seat of the Museu d'Arqueologia de Catalunya, so Iberian pots and Roman mosaics stand under Romanesque arches. The prize is the 4th-century Sepulcre de les Estacions, a sarcophagus from Empúries carved with the seasons. The cloister had a screen career too: Game of Thrones used it as the Citadel of Oldtown.
culture:Sant Pere de Galligants.why: Sit in the cloister among the carved capitals; it is the quietest corner of the north end of town.
facts: Carrer de Santa Llúcia, by the Galligants stream, at the north end of the Barri Vell

culture:Museu d'Història dels Jueus.name: Museu d'Història dels Jueus
culture:Museu d'Història dels Jueus.teaser: Eleven rooms on the people who lived, studied and were expelled from these lanes
culture:Museu d'Història dels Jueus.story: Carrer de la Força is narrow, steep and dark, and the Centre Bonastruc ça Porta sits halfway up it, named for the scholar better known as Nachmanides, born in Girona in 1194. Around him the city became one of the first centres of Kabbalah in Spain. The museum's eleven rooms move from daily life to learning, festivals and the community's end in the expulsion. You come out into the stepped alleys of one of Europe's best-preserved medieval Jewish quarters, which the walk card covers in full.
culture:Museu d'Història dels Jueus.why: Give it an hour before you wander the Call: the lanes make sense once you know who lived in them.

culture:Banys Àrabs.name: Banys Àrabs
culture:Banys Àrabs.teaser: Called Arab, built by Christians: a 12th-century Romanesque bathhouse under a ring of slim columns
culture:Banys Àrabs.story: The name misleads. These public baths were built by Christian Girona in the late 12th century, copying the plan of Roman and Islamic bathhouses: a cold room, a warm room, a hot room heated from below. The sources date the building to about 1194, some to 1198. The room everyone photographs is the apodyterium, the changing room, where a ring of slim columns holds up a small lantern over an octagonal pool and the light falls straight down onto the water. Very few civil buildings of that age survive in Catalonia.
culture:Banys Àrabs.why: Go at midday, when the sun drops through the lantern onto the octagonal pool.
facts: Carrer de Ferran el Catòlic, beside the Plaça dels Jurats, north of the cathedral

culture:Casa Masó.name: Casa Masó
culture:Casa Masó.teaser: Of all the painted houses on the Onyar, this is the one whose door opens to visitors
culture:Casa Masó.story: Rafael Masó was born in this house in 1880 and became the architect who gave Girona its Noucentisme. Between 1911 and 1919 he joined four family dwellings into one and reworked the river front, the facade you see from the bridges today. The city bought it in 2006 and the Fundació Rafael Masó shows it in groups of at most eight, so you look out of the back windows straight down onto the Onyar. The reflected houses and bridges have their own walk card.
culture:Casa Masó.why: Book ahead: it is the only chance to see the river from inside one of its houses.
facts: Carrer de les Ballesteries 29, Barri Vell

craft:Escola de Ceràmica de la Bisbal.name: Escola de Ceràmica de la Bisbal
craft:Escola de Ceràmica de la Bisbal.teaser: Put your hands in Empordà clay at the school two potters founded in 1972
craft:Escola de Ceràmica de la Bisbal.story: La Bisbal d'Empordà has fired terracotta since the Middle Ages; the clay is under the town and its main street is still lined with potteries. In 1972 the ceramicist Maria Dolors Ros and Albert Vancells opened a school here, and more than fifty years on it still teaches on working wheels and kilns. In summer it runs week-long courses open to anyone, from a first go at throwing to porcelain, with Dolors Ros herself on wheel technique in the old guide's listing. The town's Terracotta museum makes a good first stop.
craft:Escola de Ceràmica de la Bisbal.why: Book a summer week and come home with pots you threw yourself on an Empordà wheel.

craft:La Sobirana, Santa Coloma de Farne.name: La Sobirana, Santa Coloma de Farners
craft:La Sobirana, Santa Coloma de Farne.teaser: Fill a jar with green walnuts, herbs and spirit, and carry your own ratafia home to age
craft:La Sobirana, Santa Coloma de Farne.story: Santa Coloma de Farners, in the wooded Selva west of Girona, calls itself the home town of ratafia, and its liqueur makers meet in a confraria. La Sobirana, a small cooperative set up in 2018, works from a tavern-keeper's recipe of 1842 and runs a hands-on workshop with the confraria: you cut the walnuts, choose the herbs and seal your own maceration to take away. A 2019 session cost €45 and ran three hours. Missing: published dates for 2026, so you must ask the cooperative when the next session runs.

craft:Other one.name: Museu del Suro, Palafrugell
craft:Other one.teaser: Watch a cork oak stripped of its bark at dawn, then work the fresh cork in the museum's workshop
craft:Other one.story: Palafrugell was a cork town, its workshops cutting bottle stoppers from the bark of the Gavarres oaks, and the Museu del Suro tells that story. Each early summer the museum takes it outside. In its Matinals Sureres, held between mid-June and mid-July, a peler strips the bark from a living cork oak with an axe, and afterwards you sit at a bench and work the cork just taken off the tree. The coast itself is the Costa Brava guide's. Missing: anything bookable outside June and July.
craft:Other one.why: Time a June visit for a stripping morning; the smell of fresh cork is unlike anything in the museum cases.
facts: Watch the bark stripped from a cork oak, then a hands-on workshop with the fresh cork; guided museum visit, sometimes a wine tasting

craft:What is sold as local craft.name: What is sold as local craft
craft:What is sold as local craft.teaser: Girona's old town has few workshops; most 'local' pottery and trinkets were made somewhere else
craft:What is sold as local craft.story: Walk up Carrer de la Força or along the Rambla and the shelves look regional: glazed jugs, fridge magnets of the Onyar houses, fly figurines, cork coasters. Very little of it is made in the city. The glazed earthenware that reads as 'Girona pottery' comes, at best, from La Bisbal d'Empordà, about 30 km away, and a lot of cheaper ware is factory stock with no maker at all. Turn a pot over before you pay: a real La Bisbal workshop signs or stamps its pieces, and a sticker with a country of origin tells you the rest.
craft:What is sold as local craft.why: If you want Empordà pottery, buy it in La Bisbal, from the potter's own shop.
facts: Turn the piece over: look for a workshop stamp, signature or a La Bisbal name; a printed import sticker means it was not made here
Drive to La Bisbal d'Empordà and buy along its pottery street, or take Girona-made food home: anchovies, Garrotxa cheese, ratafia from Santa Coloma

linger:Espresso Mafia.name: Espresso Mafia
linger:Espresso Mafia.teaser: A white room under the Cort Reial arcades where the roaster is the furniture and there is no wifi
linger:Espresso Mafia.story: A year after La Fàbrica, in 2016, the Meiers opened their second room on Carrer de la Cort Reial, under the stone arcades. Inside it is almost clinical: white walls, the roasting kit, a custom two-group Sanremo machine, a few seats. The point is to taste. Ask for the flight and the barista will run several house roasts side by side; on a warm day take the cup outside to the bench under the arcade and watch the delivery vans squeeze past.
linger:Espresso Mafia.why: Order the tasting flight and compare the roasts; this is the room for it.

linger:Cafè Le Bistrot.name: Cafè Le Bistrot
linger:Cafè Le Bistrot.teaser: Tables climbing a flight of stone steps opposite a Gothic palace, with a crêpe and a cold glass
linger:Cafè Le Bistrot.story: Since the late 1970s the bistrot has put its tables on the Pujada de Sant Domènec, one per step, facing the Agullana palace across the stairs. Inside it feels like an old French brasserie; outside is where everyone wants to sit. It was among the first places in the city to serve crêpes, and the cod brandada filling is still the order, with a rustic pizza de pagès for the hungry. Thursday lunch brings black rice. Come in the evening when the light goes gold on the stone.

linger:Palau Fugit.name: Palau Fugit
linger:Palau Fugit.teaser: A Baroque palace reopened as a hotel, with a vermouth on the roof beside the old ramparts
linger:Palau Fugit.story: Casa Heras de Puig, an 18th-century palace left empty for years, reopened in 2023 as the 24-room Palau Fugit, reworked by El Equipo Creativo and Isern Associats. Walk in for the Yves Klein-blue reception desk under a gold chandelier and Frederic Amat's ceramic fountain, almost three metres tall, in the courtyard. Then go up: El Terrat, the roof terrace, pours vermouth and tapas in the shade of the city's oldest walls, while Gipsy downstairs mixes cocktails and has live music some nights.

linger:La Fàbrica with a laptop.name: La Fàbrica with a laptop
linger:La Fàbrica with a laptop.teaser: The cyclists' café works for a laptop only off-peak: early on a weekday, or after the lunch rush
linger:La Fàbrica with a laptop.story: Plugs are few and mid-morning the room fills with club riders, so pick your hour. A weekday at opening, before the group rides arrive, or the quiet stretch after lunch, gives you a table and a second filter without guilt. Weekends, leave the laptop on board. The café's own story is on its card in the tables.
linger:La Fàbrica with a laptop.why: Go at nine on a weekday and claim a table before the riders come in.

linger:Idle Hands.name: Idle Hands
linger:Idle Hands.teaser: Coffee, records and paintings for sale in one small room on a quiet square
linger:Idle Hands.story: Ayla Kellens, trained as a jewellery designer, fitted out this room on the Plaça Bell-lloc herself at the end of 2022 and hangs her own Costa Brava paintings on the walls, for sale. Her partner Jacob ran a roastery in Antwerp and roasts here under his Ambient label. The same space is a café, a natural-wine bar and a record shop, so a breakfast can drift towards a glass without changing tables while a record turns on the deck. Friday and Saturday nights it reopens for burgers.
linger:Idle Hands.why: Order a flat white of the Ambient roast and the shakshuka, then look at the paintings.

linger:Jardins dels Alemanys.name: Jardins dels Alemanys
linger:Jardins dels Alemanys.teaser: Shade, cats and the cathedral apse at eye level, among the ruins of old barracks on the walls
linger:Jardins dels Alemanys.story: The name means the Germans' gardens, after the soldiers once quartered in the barracks whose roofless walls still stand here. The city has planted the ruins with trees and laid gravel paths between the stones, so you sit in green rooms open to the sky. Cats sleep on the warm walls. Turn around and the apse of the cathedral is right there, close enough to read the stonework. It is a place for a book; the wall walk that passes it has its own card.
linger:Jardins dels Alemanys.why: Bring a book and take the bench facing the cathedral apse.
facts: Behind the cathedral at the top of the Barri Vell; reached by a lane east of the cathedral or from the wall walk

linger:Jardí de la Francesa.name: Jardins de la Francesa
linger:Jardí de la Francesa.teaser: A wall-top garden that shows you the back of the cathedral and its gargoyle called the witch
linger:Jardí de la Francesa.story: Up on the walls next to the Jardins dels Alemanys, this small garden of part-restored ruins and thick greenery looks at the cathedral from behind, where few visitors stand. From here you see the apse and the gargoyle Girona calls la Bruixa, the witch, jutting from the stone. A Romanesque tower, the Torre de Carlemany, rises beside it; guides disagree on whether it is the only part of the Romanesque cathedral still intact. Enclosed corners make it a good place to sit out of the wind.
linger:Jardí de la Francesa.why: Find the witch gargoyle on the cathedral wall, then sit in the quiet corner below the tower.
